question: What has been evaluated for LLMs (tasks), where (datasets and benchmarks) and how (automatic vs human), and what challenges remain?

Summary of success and failure cases of LLMs by task (Sec 6)
Summary of metrics, datasets and benchmarks (46 benchmarks) and of new evaluation protocols

limits: Survey, no experiments of its own; conclusions depend on specific datasets and on 2023-era models (ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude, Bard, LLaMA).
Authors say the benchmark list (46) is not exhaustive and the taxonomy is one of several possible.
Authors expect that online services such as Claude and ChatGPT will improve and some limitations described are mitigated; readers should rerun on current systems.
Contamination is asserted as a risk of static public benchmarks but never quantified or tested.
Dynamic testing is said to need an answer to whether it truly generates OOD examples; few studies exist (Sec 7.5).

Human-evaluation guidance is a list of factors (evaluator count, rubrics, expertise) with no procedure; LLM-as-judge is only mentioned (PandaLM, LLM-EVAL, MT-Bench winrate by GPT-4), not assessed for bias.
No agreement statistics, no sample sizes guidance.
practices: Choose the protocol per task: automatic evaluation is cheaper, more standardised and less subjective; use human evaluation where automatic metrics are unsuitable such as open generation (Sec 5).
Weigh automatic and human evaluation in combination for practical applications (Sec 5.2).

Human evaluation: set adequate number of evaluators for representation and significance, use rubrics (accuracy, relevance, fluency, transparency, safety, human alignment) and evaluators with domain expertise (Sec 5.2, Table 10).
Move toward dynamic, evolving evaluation instead of static public benchmarks because of memorisation and contamination (Sec 7.4).
Evaluate beyond accuracy: calibration, fairness, robustness (Sec 5.1, Table 9).
Evaluate the evaluation system itself for integrity and trustworthiness (Sec 7.5).
Evaluation should deliver analysis and guidance for improving the model, not only scores (Sec 7.7).
